newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH BREWERS CALL FOR LOWER BEER TAXES.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH BREWERS CALL FOR LOWER BEER TAXES.

text.p: Finnish brewers on Wednesday repeated their call for lower alcohol taxes in the face of ever mounting imports of lower-priced alcohol brought into the country by travellers.
"Alcohol tourism will continue to rise unless alcohol taxation in Finland is reduced," the Finnish federation of the brewing and soft drink industry said in a statement.
"The (brewing industry's) goal is that the beer tax should be lowered to the Swedish level which would mean cutting it in half," federation spokeswoman Sirpa Rinne said by telephone.

The brewers referred to a new study by Finnish Gallup showing that alcohol imports by private individuals rose sharply last year, with beer imports up 54 percent and spirits imports up 39 percent on 1995.
Finns now pay 7.65 markka in tax on every litre of beer, and tax now accounts for about 65 percent of the cost of a bottle of beer in Finland, Rinne said.
In the 1997 budget, the government has planned for 7.1 billion markka in tax revenues from alcohol. About 3.2 billion markka of that would come from beer taxes, Rinne said.

When reporting 1996 earnings last week, beverage group Oy Hartwall Ab said per capita consumption of beer in Finland had risen, but that the sales trend was the reverse "owing to Finland's excessively high beer tax."
In January, brewer Oy Sinebrychoff Ab said its Finnish beer sales fell 1.9 percent in 1996 and that domestic beer sales were unlikely to rise this year.

The amount of alcohol imported by travellers last year had increased despite new restrictions on travellers' duty-free imports from Russia and Estonia introduced in mid-1996, the brewers federation said.
According to the Gallup poll, 66 percent of Finns would consider a reduction in alcohol taxes "very" or "somewhat" favourable, the federation said.
Those who brought beer into the country said they would not need to go on beer-buying trips if the average price of a 0.33 litre bottle of medium-strength beer in Finland were 4.27 markka.
The average bottle price is now 5.50 markka, Rinne said.
"In terms of beer taxation this would mean reducing taxes to the level prevailing in Sweden," it said.
